en: The fivefold offerings were seen as the severed paths by means of the section on primordial wisdom.
Salutation to that Lakulin, who is the navel of all and from whom nothing is deficient.
What is the time for one who is unconditioned?
What has been proclaimed? And what mantras have been celebrated?
O Great Sage, by what agent or by what mantra is the consecration performed? What is the fruit of the consecration, and for whom is it intended?

The ritual form consists of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the implements; having consecrated the *darbha* grass with mantras, it is traditionally taught that the *svadhā* offerings belong to the gods.
The preceptor is traditionally remembered as the instrumental cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) for the performance of the consecration rite.
The substance of conditioned phenomena is the deceased; the fruit of conditioned phenomena is the authority over the course of transmigration.
The feet, hands, head, forehead, eyes, and likewise the nostrils.
Even so, one should worship Viṣṇu;
nevertheless, I shall now fully explain the supreme rite of consecration (*saṃskāra*),
by which practitioners indeed become fit.
It should be understood that eligibility for this belongs to one who has undergone refinement (saṃskṛta), and not to anyone else.
These were previously shown by Śiva and others for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa.
One who has been impelled by Śiva himself to investigate those various [teachings],
and who has approached [the teacher] properly— that Brahmin should be thoroughly examined.
One's country, caste, family, conduct, learning, and indeed one's wealth.
And for the sake of the clarity of the senses, as well as for the health of the body.

Faith, devotion to Śiva, fortitude, steadfastness, straightforwardness, enthusiasm for awakening, and spiritual power— these, O disciple, are remembered as the qualities required of one who is well-prepared.
The teachers, with the eye of knowledge, have examined [the matter];
thereafter, they have accepted it, either subsequently or preceded by a formal entry.
He abandons gold, clothing, wife, and so forth, according to his own will.
When the Guru says this,
he should then collect a tooth-stick made of Udumbara wood— smooth, unblemished, twelve finger-breadths long,
straight, with its bark intact, and fresh.
When the milk is exhausted, one's enthusiasm wanes; when the mind is crooked, one's intellect becomes crooked.
He was a border-dweller among the Sakītas and was afflicted by disease.
It is traditionally taught: one should not strike with the nails, nor should one touch [the ground] with the feet while impure.
O Brahmins, having brought that [gift] for his guru, one who is being initiated should offer it.
Then the preceptor, having taken that tooth-stick as prescribed, [should proceed].
Resorting to Dakṣiṇāmūrtti, the wise one should perform the ritual slaughter.
Having performed the ritual offering of meat according to the prescribed rules upon the previously [installed] images.
Thereafter, one should place the *argha* offering upon them with perfumes, flowers, and water.
One should diligently offer incense and cause the entirety of Śiva to inhale it;
then, having informed the Lord of Devas, the wise one should entreat the knower of mantras.
O best of gods, if this man has been purified by the descent of the vision of Śiva upon Brahmā,
then by your command I shall consecrate this most excellent of the twice-born.
But the teacher, though firm in his vows, was not recognized by the deity;
through this bond, he became possessed of mantra-power.
Having honored [the tooth-stick] with one’s head, one should recite the mantra over it once;
then, one should place the tooth-stick and other mantras according to the prescribed ritual.
One should place Sadyojāta on the head; immediately thereafter, one should place the deity Aghora; afterwards, one should place Tatpuruṣa.
Thereafter, the wise one should place Īśāna, the Lord of Devas, in the northeast.
One should perform the recitation of the Pañcabrahma mantras once at each respective station;
these are to be known here by the wise as the five sacred joints (parvan).
On the sacred festival days (parvan), one should offer flowers, perfumes, and incense here.
Having offered that which has been prepared with the five joints to the God of gods,
one should not subsequently cleanse it with ashes.
Having taken that [vessel] and having performed a circumambulation, the preceptor,
facing toward the [deity] there, should indeed bestow it upon the disciple with devotion.
It should be said: "And indeed, at dawn, having obtained a tooth-stick, one whose body is armored with mantra should perform the cleansing of the teeth with a focused mind."
Holding it with the right hand alone and facing eastward as before,
one should slowly chew the tooth-stick, but one must not let the shavings fall on the ground.
Facing east, he should not move his head;
having washed with water filtered through a cloth, he should offer it and then dismiss [the deity].
One should know that [the fire] facing downward, or turned toward the south or the southwest, is unfavorable; whereas one facing in any other direction is favorable.
Thereafter, one should observe whether what has fallen is auspicious or inauspicious;
for the sake of all accomplishments, the knower of the self, facing the direction of the preceptor, [should perform the rite].
If one has not attained clarity, one should sleep on the ground after having smeared it with cow dung.
Having seen a dream, the practitioner should report it to the preceptor.
One should never undergo initiation after seeing a bad dream;
however, one who has seen an auspicious dream may be initiated according to the prescribed rule.
On that day, he should have his hair and nails shaved;
with self-restraint, he should perform this rite on that very day.
Then, O Brahmin, having performed his bath, he should ask forgiveness from the ancestors and the gods:
"O Śivā, may the ancestors and the gods forgive me; I have returned to my own state."
One should not speak harshly to a person who is unrighteous, nor to one who is not a Brahmin, nor to one who is not a stranger; one should not speak words that cause anger.
One should bring sandalwood paste, perfumes, incense, and white flowers; indeed, Sāravaṭī brings all these here in their entirety.
The vessels for the water-offering (*arghapātra*) may be made of clay or of silver.
Having gathered leaves, one should make them sleepless (? and firm;
the vessels for the *argha* offering should certainly be made from *daṃśadvencā*.
And one should carry away the ashes from there, as well as the consecrated water-pots.
The auspicious fragrant *pavitraka* should be prepared for the Trimūrti;
in the absence of thread, one should make it with *kuśa* grass or with flowers from an auspicious place. Having gathered all these materials on a meritorious day, the preceptor [should proceed].
Having consecrated it with five mantras, one should employ it according to its own ritual procedure.
Tranquil, bathed in ashes, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses.
But the wise one possesses the eye of knowledge, having destroyed his impurities through austerity and other means.
He was vigilant, meditating on Śiva, learned in the scriptures, and endowed with compassion.
O noble teacher, grant me the mantra; may I attain the imperishable Śiva.
Having draped the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) over the mirror, the water-pitchers, the altar, and likewise the yogic seat, one should then perform the ritual action.
The preceptor himself should bathe the deity, together with the altar, with water purified by mantras,
and likewise cleanse the yoga-pīṭha.
And one should offer the vessels for the *argha* oblation to all the forms in their respective order.
They are destroyers of sin, meritorious, and indeed increasers of dharma.
The southern, the eastern, the northern, and likewise the western;
the southeastern, the northwestern, and the north-easterly are thus remembered as the fourfold [directions].
Nairṛtī, as well as the Nāgī, and Śiva are remembered as the ten forms.
The southern direction is called Yāmyā, and the eastern direction is designated as Aindrī.
The northern form is indeed known as Saumya, and the western is remembered as Vāruṇī.
The southeastern direction is Āgneyī; likewise, the northeastern direction is Īśānī.
The subsequent [direction] is the western, the lower is the south-western, and the further is the southern.
The upper form is remembered as Dhruvā, while they declare the lower one to be Nāgī.
For these are proclaimed as meritorious in all the ordinances of sacrifice;
and one should carefully place the vessels for the *argha* offering, which are the embodiment of all forms.
One should indeed place there the five objects of knowledge and the *argha* vessel itself.
The wise practitioner should then prepare the vessel for the arghya offering and the yoga-pīṭha.
One should arrange the arghya vessels and fill them with scented water;
then the preceptor should offer the three forms [of the deity] upon the head of Śiva.
With effort, [one should perform this] in all forms, sequentially in the argha vessels.
Then, indeed, he gradually touched him from the side in those very forms.
One should offer the arghya vessels according to the rule, accompanied by the mantras.
He should bring all the water-pots as well as the yoga-seat.
Having meditated upon the illustrious Lakulīśāna in every single form, he becomes a knower of Yoga.
Having diligently offered the *argha* water, accompanied by the recitation of the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahma*).
And flowers, as well as purificatory items of every kind, according to the prescribed rule.
Having given those [offerings] into the half-filled bowls, he should then touch them together.
Having touched the Lord of the Gods in each of his forms in successive order.
And having offered the arghya according to the rule, he should likewise offer it to those very forms of Śiva.
One should first bathe the deity with sacred ash and afterwards with auspicious waters;
having bathed the Lord with jars of meritorious water, one should then anoint him with fragrant pastes.
Having performed worship with auspicious flowers, one should offer fragrant sacred threads.
Whoever should worship the Supreme Lord according to this procedure,
For that preeminent practitioner, the yoga of Śiva proceeds;
having thus performed the ritual touching of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Having exerted oneself with great effort in the yoga of purifying the disciple,
this yoga of ritual purification must then be performed for both the deity and the disciple.
At the time of renunciation, the Hand of Śiva is prescribed for the disciple who has been properly purified with ashes according to the scriptures after bathing.
Having meditated with devotion upon Śiva in the form of the Guru who bears the illustrious Lakula,
the wise practitioner should again meditate on His hand placing it upon the head of the seeker; having properly performed the renunciation of substances, states of being, and the internal fire.
Then, one should perform the cutting of the topknot with the hand of Śiva, accompanied by the mantra.
The head of Śiva, consisting of the three forms (trimūrti), should lead the crest-lock of the practitioner.
This Hand of Śiva, composed of the five Brahmans, is drawn forth by the heart-mantra.
These three—the substance, the state of being, and the fire—are the three acts to be severed by the three [edges].
Therefore, one should constantly cultivate the state of Śiva through the actions of speech and mind.
With that very [blade], one should cut the crest-lock (śikhā) from the head of the practitioner;
one should not cut it with iron, nor with the fingernails, nor likewise should one tear it out.
And a name should be given that is auspicious and impelled by Śiva;
then, impelled by Śiva, he should place two flowers upon the disciple for the removal of sins.
One should cause him to meditate upon the mantras and constantly instruct him in the ritual procedure;
for one who is blind to the ritual requirements due to ignorance, one should prescribe purification.
This very same procedure is prescribed for the initiation of the practitioner as well;
however, there may be a specific placement of the feet at the end, or otherwise, due to contradiction.
Furthermore, there is conciliation, inquiry, and the self-surrender to the Guru.
Having grasped it, one should examine it; refinement is the fitness for the ritual procedure.
For erudition is their seventh station, which is worthy of honoring the guru.
This detailed procedure should also be understood to apply to the consecration of the practitioner;
indeed, by traversing just seven steps, one attains victory over the seven worlds.
Thus ends the procedure for the consecration.
Having accepted an alms-bowl, a water-strainer, a garment, or any other implement for the practice of Dharma, the ascetic should purify them by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).

One should perform [the rite] one hundred times for a Śūdra woman, fifty times for a Vaśyā, and likewise ten times for a Kṣatriyā; for a Vaiśya woman it is ten, and for a Brāhmaṇa woman it is proclaimed to be ten.

If there is a breach of purity, one should perform a hundred [repetitions]; likewise if there is a breach of the vessel. Indeed, having eaten from broken vessels, one must thereafter observe a three-day fast.
Having set aside the remnants of his alms, the ascetic who is devoted to self-restraint should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) with each morsel of food.
Alternatively, one should perform whatever the guru says, without hesitation.
The teacher alone is the cause everywhere for both punishment and favor.
Having accepted gold, sesame seeds, cows, land, wealth, or women as gifts, one who lacks self-control falls; of this there is no doubt.
Having abandoned all that wealth, one should then observe three fasts;
by reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one shall thereafter attain purification.
Having stolen ashes, an earthen vessel, clothes, a needle, a thimble, a water-pot,
or a skull-bowl, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
But he who, having gone forth into homelessness, does not even speak with those born into sensual enjoyments, nor touches them even by measure— [he is truly a renunciant].
Whatever has been touched by him, or whatever was in his possession, one should know that to be unfit for consumption; having eaten such food, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
But he who, having become a wanderer, falls away even once—
that fallen one may indeed be purified by avoiding the company of such a vessel.
When [the disciple] has come and the bowl has been produced, it would then be beyond conversation.
By the mere use of such a bowl, one would go to hell for that duration.
That ascetic who, from the very beginning, should even once break his vessel, one should know him to be a non-ascetic;
though he lives by the outward mark, he is merely a twice-born man.
When a confluence of all sins has arisen, one should perform renunciation; having abandoned them, one should maintain what remains.
Then, having shed tears and renounced all accumulated wealth,
one who has traveled a hundred yojanas is liberated from that sin.

If a practitioner undergoes cutting, piercing, or cooking, having touched such impurity, the purification of a *preta* is prescribed. Or, if a twice-born man is seen performing either improper conduct (*ayoga*) or ritual application (*prayoga*), [he must likewise purify himself].
One is born among the animal wombs for sixty thousand years.
One who first speaks with intention, but later acts without intention, and who,
through attachment to the defects of sense objects, fails to restrain himself— that ascetic shall go to hell.
If one who has fallen away from the life of a wandering mendicant undertakes a religious observance, all of that becomes fruitless for him; even though he has performed it, he shall go to hell.

He who, though himself without marks (aliṅgin), lives off the livelihood of those who possess marks (liṅgin) by assuming the form of a mark, takes away [the merit] of those with marks; therefore, he shall go to hell.
Even after committing thousands of sins and passing through various wombs, one who has attained Śaṅkara through devotion and remains eternally united with Rudra does not perish.
If one obtains wealth that is free from fault, it is indeed a faultless alms for dharma, received unasked;
there, the yogi should practice such unprepared alms-gathering, remaining free from the falsehood of rejection.
Alms that have been set aside and brought forth, not previously solicited,
may even those who have performed evil deeds accept from a householder, for Prajāpati has so ordained.
If one who has collected alms through delusion and other such faults should abandon them out of anger or greed, that high-souled one’s act of begging is a mere mockery.
One should avoid [water] drawn even from a well that belongs to a menstruating woman, a eunuch,
a heretic, an unchaste woman, or a barren woman.
Deceit, guile, hypocrisy, causing dissension between men and women, and extortion—
one should avoid these five defects of begging. Whatever action may be performed in a base manner, or that which causes spiritual distress to the yogi, [should be avoided].
One who always possesses a wicked intention is indeed called a deceiver. || 28 ||
People constantly deceive one who administers counterfeit medicine or employs fraudulent mantras; that act is called "deception" (dambhana).
A monk who delights in sharing always brings four things to pass:
he gladdens the giver, himself, and the recipient to whom he gives.
Since Brahman is cooked by that [activity],
it partakes of the impurity of passion (*rajas*) through its desire for enjoyment;

he who is intent on this is a householder by the distinction of cooking, a monk (*bhikṣu*) by the distinction of the feet, and a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) by the distinction of the [remaining] stages.
[This is] for the one who has gone forth (*yati*). Among those [faults], that which is glorious... by that there is further increase...
mixing (*saṃkara*), and the breaking of mixed vessels is fivefold: medicinal herbs, storage, the seven knowledges (*sapta-jñāna*), and so forth... this which is... the sevenfold [set].

Whatever [food] he places among the Śrāddha offerings, and likewise in storage, whether it be during the fortnight (pakṣa) [of impurity], or through confusion and corruption— whatever rule he may observe while eating the remnants of such [impure] food, the Rākṣasas [seize him] by that very action.

When one who eats from a vessel covers the vessels separately with the edge [of his garment], he attains either Brahman or Viṣṇu; for him who properly washes those [vessels] first, that very act in the sacrifice is as excellent as the best oblation.
Having collected alms in his bowl, he should not ask for anything at all from the three corners of the path, except for water from a well or from wood.
Her vessels are non-metallic, free from cracks, and without blemishes;
their purification with water is prescribed to be performed just like that of the *camasa* cups.
Manu Svāyambhuva declared that vessels made of gourd, wood, metal, clay, as well as leaves, and woven fiber— these indeed are the vessels to be employed.
One should abandon vessels made of clay, wood, or fruit that have been touched by phlegm, urine, feces, blood, or semen.
A vessel that has been touched by a thief, a *cāṇḍāla*, an outcaste, crows, feces, and so forth, or which a dog has licked, should be abandoned; this applies even to vessels made of precious gems.
I must be thoroughly examined when acting as a ritual assistant (sphoṭāyan) or in water;
or rather, the wise man should avoid him when he is an unfit recipient (upahata).
One should purify it by rubbing with a *karṣa* of earth and removing all oiliness;
having washed it with cow-hair, one should sprinkle it thoroughly with the *trikoṇa* [mantra].
If, while washing, oil should happen to adhere to the vessel through negligence,
one should wash that vessel thoroughly and then smear it with mantras alone.
When a monk who eats from his alms-bowl is severely afflicted by diseases, then, remaining composed and established in equanimity, the wise one should disregard the illness.
Whatever suffering is internal, or indeed physical suffering arising from external elements, or that which is called suffering caused by fate— a wise person should endure all of it.

The fivefold mendicant's alms are traditionally recorded as: that which is collected like honey from many flowers (mādhūkaraka), that which is obtained without prior intention (asaṃkalpa), that which was previously prepared (prāk-vṛtta), that which is unasked for (ayācita), and that which is obtained at the proper time (kālopapanna).
Wandering from house to house, one should not avoid any dwelling;
however, having heard the report of others, one should shun a house that is wicked.
If a virtuous mendicant should transgress against one who has fallen but remains blameless,
he gives away that person's merit and takes upon himself their demerit.
Likewise, if a mendicant should approach a householder while being free from desire, [the householder should offer alms].
Taking from him both his sacrificial merit (iṣṭa) and his works of public utility (pūrta), that mendicant departs—
he who is always restrained by his vows and ever devoted to self-restraint (yama).
Being equal toward honor and dishonor, he is worthy to eat from the alms-bowl.
He whose mind has become melted into the state free from passion and the like,
who is devoid of longing for all worldly activities, is worthy to eat from the alms-bowl.
The yogi who possesses no longing for the enjoyments of desire,
who is free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, is worthy to eat from the alms-bowl.
He who is pure, a devotee of Śiva, and devoted to recitation and meditation; who has conquered sleep and worldly attachments, and is constant—such a person deserves to eat from a sacred vessel.
One who is always devoted to solitary conduct, who is supremely gentle toward all,
and whose mind is ever serene, deserves to eat from a worthy vessel.

One whose self-attachment and anger have departed, who is wise and devoted to Brahman, who has renounced worldly undertakings, and who is versatile— such a person deserves to eat from a worthy vessel. Indeed, one who is vigilant, who has conquered his vital breaths, who is devoted to the guru, and who is free from deceit [is likewise fit].
The yogi, like the wind, may eat from anywhere, provided it is in a proper vessel.
One who is habituated to bathing at the three junctions of the day, who wears little clothing, who is well-resolved,
and who always delights in solitude, deserves to eat from a vessel.
One who avoids external light, who does not disdain leftovers, who wears the remains of offerings as garlands, and whose body is smeared with ashes, is worthy to eat from a vessel.
Regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, always intent on alms and a seat,
free from anger, wise, and mindful— he is worthy to eat from his bowl.
Having washed the bowl until it is stainless before the image, he should treat it like a sacred book.

One should not constantly cleanse oneself with cow-hair; one shall not thereby attain purity. Whatever merit is obtained from a thousand horse-sacrifices properly performed, that same fruit one attains by feeding a worthy recipient for a single day.

The Brahmins who discourse upon the Veda declare that for one who has conquered the senses and who, being pure, eats whatever is placed in the vessel, that very act constitutes the fruit [of his merit].
[It protects him] from great and terrible fears, and from hells that are difficult to cross.
It delivers [us] from all sounds; this is the vessel for him.
One should not use medicine, a tooth-stick, drinking water,
or water for rinsing the mouth at times other than during meals.
Having stayed for one night, the ascetic should abandon his bowl and staff.
One should completely renounce the staff-mantra (daṇḍamantra).
He who drinks water from a vessel after having eaten half a meal [is guilty].
By that, the deity, the vessel, and oneself would be destroyed.
Thus ends the procedure for the vessel.
The wise preceptor, having taken white flowers, [should proceed].
Having prostrated with his head before Śiva, he should slowly approach the presence of the disciple.
Having placed those flowers into the hollowed palms of the brahmin.
Then, having taken [the substance] with the two syllables "aṃ" and "aṣṭābhyām," one should bring it into the presence of Śiva.
Having offered a handful of flowers, O Rudra, one should present the practitioner;
having recited the five mantras once, one should then make a request to Śiva.
Having informed the omniscient Lord and seated him upon an excellent throne,
the Guru smeared the major and minor limbs and the joints of his body with ashes;
having applied them to those very parts of the body, he bound [the ashes] firmly.
Having offered flowers according to the rule, one should also cleanse the triple line on all sides, as well as the hands, the topknot, the eightfold form, and the area above the forehead.
The ears, cheeks, eyes, nostrils, and likewise the chin; the neck and heart in the joints of the breasts; and the throat in the incision of the arteries.
The shoulders, the armpits, the space between the armpits, the firm hips, the flanks, the joints of the sides, the buttocks, the thighs, the shanks, and the knees. 81
All the knots on the sides, the feet, and the tips of the feet as well.
One should also purify with mantras whatever else there may be, such as marrow, semen, and so forth.
Then, having informed the Lord of Devas, one should thereafter offer the water consecrated by mantras.
Afterwards, having seated [him] on an excellent seat, one should perform a circumambulation from left to right.
The wise one should purify it as before with ritual substances;
furthermore, the touching [of the vessel] must be performed correctly so that purity is produced.
One becomes pure by drinking [water] that has been rendered free from external impurities.
All of those become pure by means of the auspicious ashes of Śiva.
Having performed the touching in this manner, he took recourse to the southern form.
One who knows the ritual procedure should [anoint] with ashes purified by mantras, and indeed with mantras themselves.
Having thus touched the Brahmin, one should again give him ash-water for the sake of purifying the internal defects born of seed and womb. This procedure,
however, is to be undertaken afterwards in due order.

Homage be to Lakulīśa, the illuminator of the meaning of the five-fold purpose, who transcends all, endowed with the two powers, and possessed of immeasurable splendor. Now, therefore, I shall fully expound the supreme procedure for atonement.
For Brahmins who are seekers of liberation and are not negligent regarding their restraints (yama) and observances (niyama),
the wise should not prescribe the rules for atonement (prāyaścitta) as if they were ordinary people;
rather, their purification— both external and internal— is accomplished through the threefold utterances of the sacred syllables.
Just as they say that the external and internal expiation consists of three parts, so too,
for the sake of the disciple's welfare, he has declared both the external expiation and the internal one;
therefore, the external and internal expiation must be understood.
Having observed the succession of negligence beginning with the lack of protection,
some authoritative teachers have stated regarding this *Pañcārthadarśana*:
"In all cases of transgression, a triple [punishment] must be applied according to the rule."
The threefold [means] has a visible purpose; through the designation of that which has a visible purpose, the wise one possesses the threefold [means];
and by means of the mention of that which has an invisible purpose, there is the supreme tradition.
Therefore, the method of yoga should be performed constantly until the end.
One should perform the unseen purpose through the practice of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
which has been taught by other learned teachers; that [practice] must be carried out by the wise for the removal of impurity according to the correct ritual procedure.
But it has been said by those virtuous ones who speak what is beneficial:
"This praise of human immersion is for the sake of external and internal purity;
internal purity comes from the placement [of mantras] upon the body, while physical purity on the limbs comes from ashes."
What should one who is well-versed in the sacred tradition do for the sake of purifying sins such as violence?
When another transgression has occurred,
one should perform this rite accompanied by charity, sacrifice, and austerity, along with bathing and other purifications.
Through this procedure, there arises the fitness of the purified person for liberation from the bond of merit.
"I shall not speak to one who is impure; he would practice deceit toward me.

Even if a man, through lack of desire, extreme delusion, or being under the sway of evil karma, should act thus—even if he is wise, discerning, and possessed of excellent purity—he might fall into negligence."
The practitioner should be immeasurable, peaceful, of virtuous conduct, and endowed with compassion.
One who is dispassionate and has sought refuge should be purified by means of penances.
One should always practice with proper application during the night in the portion of Yama.
One should always practice deceit and follow the prescribed rule when censuring others.
The Sage declared that this fitness belongs to one who is pure, not to one who is impure;
therefore, one should perform this ritual procedure with a pure mind.
The virtuous have proclaimed here the ritual procedure that brings about the destruction of sins accumulated over many births; it is the means of atonement in this very life.
For one who constantly practices the restraints (yamas) and especially the observances (niyamas),
yet also performs deceitful acts, are the restraints and the rest not rendered fruitless?
These [practices] are clearly not fruitless; they manifestly bring about purity and growth when performed with devotion toward the mind and body by men who have overcome deceit.

With a one-pointed mind and fixed upon that, he should constantly perform the rite with its prescribed method, by which dharma quickly arises, bestowing the fruit of the yoga of steadfastness. Whether through lack of desire or through negligence, he should destroy any transgression that has arisen.

Having requested from Maheśvara the specific expiations for each of the manifest sins, the ascetic himself should perform their removal through perfectly complete penances prescribed by trustworthy and most excellent brahmins.
If one who constantly performs the prescribed rites, such as the ash-bath and other vows,
should suffer a lapse through the fault of delusion, he must then perform an expiation.
The threefold downfall is said to arise from speech, mind, and body;
it is threefold, consisting of the mental, the verbal, and the physical.
And verbal sin is more grievous than the faults of mental sin.
It is declared that verbal and physical [offenses] are the most serious among faults;
and for each of these three kinds of sin,
the expiation is known to be progressively greater according to the specific nature of the act— thus spoke the sage to the Brāhmaṇa.

For mental [sins], a triad of rites should be performed; for those committed by the body, however, there is expiation. And for sins acquired in other births, the prescribed method leads to their destruction.
Through bodily defects born of past actions, a man may attain various states of birth.
Through verbal [sins] one attains the state of a bird or a beast, and through mental [sins], the state of the lowest castes.
Having heard of the defects of those things produced by the three types of action,
the wise preceptor, after examining and scrutinizing them thoroughly, should subsequently declare their purity;
having considered both the gravity and the lightness of what has been uttered with equanimity.
For the purification of that [sin], whatever has been performed by many people should be undertaken;
and having deliberated again and again, O Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas,
an atonement (prāyaścitta) must then be granted for the purification of the sin of those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin).
Thus ends the chapter on the determination of relationship, containing the expiations taught by Gārgya’s feet.
That which has not been consecrated with the mantras and has not been offered to Śambhu is unfit for bathing; it is traditionally held that the other [type] is fit for it.
He who has bathed with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) does not truly bathe even with ashes;
having reached the state of purification (niḥkṛti), he becomes pure through penance (prāyaścitta).
One whose self is joined with negligence and laziness shall fall from the ash-bath;
or, one who is deprived of the proper time for bathing shall fall from the ash-bath.
For one who is deprived of the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), this shall be the expiation.
One should perform a hundred circumambulations and recite the Raudrī mantra thousands of times;
this is declared as the expiation for one who is negligent in all the observances, such as sleeping [during the ritual],
by Purāṇakula Pāṇi.
Having traveled a hundred yojanas, the expiation for that [transgression] is as follows:
for twelve days, O son, it must be offered daily as before.
This [result] for a year would be this same amount combined with the distance traveled on the road,
doubled or even tripled according to the number of *yojanas* in sequence.
Upon the emission of semen, one should perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Being pure and composed, one should recite the Śrīkaṇṭha-rodra mantra.
This reality is to be understood at the beginning of the night, never during the day.
When the emission of semen occurs during the day, this expiation shall take place.
Having recited the Raudrī mantra fifty thousand times according to the prescribed rule,
one should likewise offer that same number of parched grains (lājās) in the temple of Śiva.
Furthermore, by drinking unpurified water, one should recite it five hundred times.
The mantra characterized by Aghora then brings about purification;
one’s eating and drinking should take place at night, and the expiation becomes progressively more effective.
One hundred circumambulations and one thousand recitations of the Raudrī mantra should be performed.
If living beings are constantly killed while wandering during the day,
whether through ignorance or negligence, no purification occurs without expiation;
one should perform six rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recite [the mantra] three hundred times.
Observing the vow, one should do so with the Raudra mantra and according to the mental sequence.
A distinction in purification is proclaimed due to the conjunction of two periods of impurity;
when such a distinction in purification has arisen, this expiation shall take place.
Having performed one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should then recite the Raudrī mantra one hundred times;
by reciting it, one attains purity, and being pure, one may perform the ritual procedure.
But when a breakage of the bowl occurs, the previous expiation shall take place.
Then, for one month, the sage should consume three morsels daily, one at a time.
A distinction of vessels is to be understood regarding the seven types of violations of the vow:
during hospitality, sacrifices, śrāddha rites, and likewise when [the food] is present nearby.
The evil-minded one eats again from a vessel that has already been sprinkled and rinsed.
In the case of *laulpa* (confusion), which is a mixture of impurities, there are seven types of "breaking the vessel" (*pātrabheda*).
When one who eats from a vessel causes the flavors to flow separately from the vessel,
he is a "breaker of the vessel" (*sapātrabhedaka*) and is censured among those who speak the Veda for a month.

A householder who [eats] with a different cooking pot and a mendicant who eats from a different vessel is born among the animal wombs for ten thousand years. This applies even to a wise sage who has remained for twelve days with his limbs covered in kusha grass.
I declare that for twelve days, the expiation shall be performed according to the reckoning of time:
a hundred circumambulations of Śambhu and a thousand recitations of the Rudra-mantra must be offered day by day by the yogin.
If one eats or drinks without having first worshipped Śiva, there must be an expiation.
A thousand jars of water, accompanied by ten thousand recitations, [is equal to the merit].
Because he remains seated on the same seat and so forth with those who have fallen [from their caste], he must perform penance once again.
He performed the Prājāpatya rite a thousand times.
Having previously practiced subsisting on alms for three days,
the sage should remain for twelve days engaged in the Prājāpatya penance.

From sharing food, beds, vehicles, contact, and common vessels, great calamities spread; they do not perish even when surrounded by those [remedies]. O King, just as a monarch [acts] toward his subjects, so too does he act toward the gods and the divine attendants.
Whatever has been eaten or drunk shall be properly digested; this is said to be his atonement.
Having performed the *saṃtarpaṇa* (satisfying rite) with water, he should then drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
By subsisting on alms for three months, he becomes purified.
O King, for the consumption of food and drink belonging to those who have died, this expiation is prescribed:
one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa rite.
Having prepared the morsels of food joined with abundant ghee and preceded by the *ghṛtāpośāna* rite, one should consume them— consecrated by mantras and known as "the blissful"—
at the beginning of the fortnight, for one night at dawn, with the senses restrained.
And one should increase the morsels from morsel to morsel, and likewise decrease them in successive stages.
Performing this Cāndrāyaṇa, one should recite the Tṛca once; at the beginning of each fortnight, following the sequential order, one worships Śiva at its conclusion.
Having offered a thousand ladles [of water] upon the head of the Liṅga and having worshipped it with devotion, the wise man should then say at the end: "Forgive me."
O Śaṅkara, whatever has been performed contrary to the rules, whether through ignorance or even knowingly, you ought to forgive all of that for me who am like a beast.
Then, having realized this, the sage himself should immediately perform emesis.
Then, having performed the Prājāpatya penance, one should first practice the three-fold [rite];
thereafter, by drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and worshipping Śiva, one becomes purified. This applies even if the food and drink of Kāpālikas have been consumed or drunk.
One should first observe fasting for three days, and thereafter perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Then, having asked the Lord of Gods for forgiveness and having worshipped him again with devotion with a hundred jars of water, one becomes pure by reciting the *Trikam* three times.
It may be thus in one way, and in two ways it becomes double;
in three ways it is declared to be triple, and in four ways it is the interval between the higher and lower.
Having understood this, for one who speaks merely [what is known], the atonement is to give half.

O Sage, for one who eats the food and drink of Buddhists who have abandoned their vows, the wise prescribe the Cāndrāyaṇa penance of the dark fortnight; however, for one who performs asceticism accompanied by the three-fold [restraints],
the Prājāpatya penance is ordained.
Having offered a thousand water-pots upon the head of the Liṅga,
the sage should then recite the Rudra-mantra twenty thousand times.
Half of what was vomited should be given away, along with a quarter-measure of black pepper and long pepper;
it should be accompanied by a water-pot for the afflicted, joined with ten thousand recitations of the mantra,
and followed by one day of fasting and three days of subsisting on alms.
The daily practice of the *Tṛka* is proclaimed as the "Black Foot" (*pādakṛṣṇa*).
Having consumed anything in contact with the property of the gods and so forth, one should perform the *Sāṃtapana* penance.
For eating food or drink from one who has fallen from their vows, purification is achieved through fasting.
A thousand circumambulations accompanied by ten million prostrations.
One should understand [the result] from drinking as half [the duration], and from eating, it shall be tenfold.
Six thousand recitations of the mantra, three hundred circumambulations,
and six thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī with six kṛśanas [of gold]— for one who desires the two-fold [attainment], these are performed by means of three hundred circumambulations.
During times of famine, when there is no gain, and in all such difficult circumstances,
one who is unable [to provide much] may show favor by giving half a measure of grain or food out of devotion.
Having eaten food from a single source, one should perform five hundred recitations;
thus endowed with the ten [observances], I am [established].

Having eaten the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of an oil-presser, the food of a cowherd, the food of a cook, or the food of a washerman, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

A woman who has been remarried, one who acts as she pleases, or one who wanders at will— if one eats from their first pregnancies, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; likewise, having eaten, drunk, or accepted anything daily in the house of such women for four years, one must perform the same.
He should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; thus he obtains the direct and perfect bestowal.
Thereafter, he attains [the goal] as before.
He shall obtain it.
One should prepare a black cloth (*kṛṣṇa*) provided with three threads for the one who has eaten;
then, having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, he attains [his state].
By the falling of the water from the *prapā*, he should mutter the *raudrī* mantra a thousand times.
Having performed one hundred and one circumambulations, she attained purity. Furthermore,
the washerman, the *rāḍa*, the fisherman, and the *bhillas*— these are currently considered the lowest-born (*antyajas*).
And one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance in the houses of these [persons],
as well as in those of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*), after drinking water [from them] that is joined with the three [impurities] every day.
Having performed three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances along with the *trika*, the observer of the Śiva-vow,
having placed a jar full of *gaḍuka* on the head of the *aliṅgin*,
and then having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and worshipped Śiva at dawn;
Having eaten food from the company of Cāṇḍālas and having drunk [their water], one should perform two prostrations joined with the *Ṛk*; thus one becomes an ascetic (*yati*).
One should offer water-pots according to one's ability upon the head of the *liṅga*;
then, having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and worshipped Śiva, one becomes purified.
From the offering of food, O Lord, there may arise a prior physical form;
having offered a single *saṅguḍaka* soaked in clarified butter, accompanied by a hundred thousand prostrations (*jaṅgha-lakṣa*), upon the head of the Liṅga.
Then, having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and worshipped Śiva, one becomes purified.

It is recorded that having eaten or drunk in the house of those who have not performed expiation (aniḥkṛti), one incurs the same [penalty] as for Cāṇḍālas; beyond that, there is no greater [sin]. Thus ends the second chapter in the Gārgyapādāpadikṣā-prāyaścittavidhi.

One who stands firm in their vow should perform penance for the following acts committed against a guru: disobeying his command, causing distraction, speaking ill of him, or piercing his vital points.
Having offered a thousand jars upon the head of the Liṅga,
one should perform twenty thousand recitations and half as many circumambulations.
Having shown disrespect to the Guru, no atonement is prescribed.
For one who betrays his guru is indeed unfit to converse with and excluded from the ritual row; however,
those others who have been previously initiated and are knowers of all the tantras should always be saluted, praised, and honored according to one's ability.
An elder woman, when reviled, may grant expiation in progressively increasing measures:
one thousand circumambulations and twenty thousand recitations of the mantra;
however, this must be determined by considering the gravity or lightness of the offense according to its specific nature.
Having reflected upon what is just and unjust, and according to the sequence of the aged and the young,
one who stands firm in their vow, having taken up the sacred water for the *arghya* offering,
shall perform thirty thousand recitations and three circumambulations, and thus becomes purified.
I shall describe, according to what was spoken by Śiva, the expiation for the intentional killing of all classes of living beings, as taught by the Sage: namely, those born from a womb,
those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and likewise those born from a sprout.
These four kinds of living beings must never be killed;
it has been declared that even the smallest among the small is like the radiance of the sun.
For the end of faults is indeed the supreme speech; having performed [this], they go to the state of the accomplished one. Likewise, the two sons of Raudrī are purified by the six limbs.
Having seen one who is pure and traveling on a journey, an ascetic devoted to Yama should recite the Raudrī mantra two thousand times; he becomes purified through the six bodily postures (āyāmas).
Furthermore, by performing fire oblations (homa), giving gifts, and kindling the sacrificial fire, O Śikhā, [one is purified].
Accompanied by a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), the recitation should be joined with *Śivā* and so forth. For men, one should perform eight hundred recitations of the *Gāyatrī*;
for the remaining [classes] and those who are hostile, one should increase it further and further.
For the sake of killing each individual species of boneless living beings,
there should be a recitation accompanied by six breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*).
For the sake of killing each individual species of bone-bearing living beings, [the same applies].
When one thousand recitations are performed together with ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), it becomes a "thousand-fold" rite.
For each killing of large birds such as vultures and the like,
this recitation must be performed two hundred times along with ten thousand oblations of fragrant substances.
For the killing of each individual pig and so forth, one should offer twenty thousand oblations to Raudrī; half of that number are prescribed as *gaḍukas*.
For the killing of each individual fish, tortoise, and so forth—
For Raudrī, twenty thousand recitations are prescribed; for Gaḍukā, half of that is remembered.
For the killing of each individual among the deer, such as the hariṇa and others, ten thousand recitations are to be performed.
Twenty thousand recitations are prescribed for Raudrī; half of that is said to be the number for Gaḍukā.

For the killing of each individual among bears, monkeys, and the like, purification is achieved by reciting [the mantra] thirty thousand times; according to the *Ṣaḍvaktra*, it shall be equal to six [such acts].

For the killing of each individual among donkeys, wild asses (*deśarā*?), and so forth, purification is achieved by reciting [the mantra] thirty thousand times; this is the purification for the six [types of animals].
For the killing of each individual among elephants, rhinoceroses (*gaṇḍaka*), and so forth...

It is taught that for each individual killing of cows, gayals, and the like, as well as for each individual killing of all animals, forty thousand recitations (*japya*) of the *gaḍuka* mantra [beginning with] *maḥ* must be performed.
Purification by means of six ten-thousand recitations of the *gaḍuka* is prescribed when there is *sāma*.
For the killing of each and every one of all the Cāṇḍālas,
purification is traditionally held to consist of six recitations of the [Gāyatrī] mantra accompanied by a thousand [prostrations].
For the killing of each and every one of all those belonging to the [first] three classes (*varṇas*),
purification is traditionally taught to be achieved by seven recitations (*japya*) combined with *gr̥dhukasra* [offerings].
And for the killing of each and every one of all *śūdras*, [the same applies].

Purification is declared to occur through eighty thousand recitations when the *gaḍuka* [vessel] is equal to the *srasa*; purification is not declared to occur through *prata* [recitations] when the *gaḍuka* is equal to the *srasa*.
For the killing of each individual among all Kṣatriyas,
purification is declared to be achieved by ten thousand recitations of the *japa* or by an equal number of *gaḍukas*.
And for the killing of each individual among all children, [the same applies].
It is taught that for each individual act of killing, there are twelve [rebirths] in the hells,
equal in number to the drops [of water], as well as for all [acts of killing] collectively;
likewise for the killing of those who possess fortitude, those with marks, and those wearing sectarian signs.
Neither the gods nor Śiva, nor even the Lord of the Kula, have declared an expiation for one who,
having been instructed in the ritual of penance by the feet [of the Guru],
should nevertheless drink liquor or cause it to be opened for drinking.
In the sequence of the *krama-śāna* rites, the pedestal (*liṅgavedī*) is established in due order.
When the *liṅga* is tilted sideways, one should provide a fivefold protrusion (*gaḍu*). When the *liṅga* has fallen [downward], one should provide eleven *madhuka* [offerings].
If [the water] falls within the distance of one cubit (*hasta*), one should give thirty;
if within two cubits, one should give five hundred;
and if within three cubits, one should give seven thousand.
Where there is a Śivaliṅga made of the flesh and fat of a Gaḍuka, at the place where your four cubits fall,
the expiation for that Śivaliṅga shall be equal to a thousand jars of water at its conclusion.
One who is devoid of the Vedas becomes a twice-born outcast through a downfall;
expiation for that prior fall occurs by assuming the form of a *liṅga* or other such [ascetic] emblems.
Thus, having understood [the matter] according to the measurement of a cubit, one should remain diligent in its application.
The four-fold *liṅga* should be proclaimed as the cave (*guhā*).
When there is a light blow, it is said to be light; when heavy, it becomes more grave. [One should avoid] the places of death and the soft [spots].

(****) Specifically regarding the defects of the *liṅga* and through combat, one should administer a harsh penance for a harsh [offense]; [the penance] is declared to be performed after [the offense] has been confessed. Thus, the penance is prescribed for one who has prostrated at the feet. (***).
Now I shall fully declare the expiation for lingas according to their number,
written in sequence upon the altar.
If a linga consisting of the essence of Śiva should split into two parts at the point of the sesame seed, [the following applies].
By thousands [of repetitions], the *gaḍuka* attains purity.
If the sign of those whose hatred has burst forth is of the nature of Śiva,
then there is no doubt that [the state] will arise there.
Now, if there should be a venerable [image] within the Linga whose nature is Śiva;

If a liṅga as small as a sesame seed is clearly manifest as being of the nature of Śiva, then what need is there for ten thousand water-pots [to purify] that liṅga? Now, [if it is already pure], why [use] the pots upon the liṅga?

Or even if [the defect] occurs in the lower part of the *liṅga* consisting of Śiva, [one should perform the rite]; there, with thirteen water-pitchers (*kumbha*), one should [purify] the *liṅga*. If the stationary *śivaliṅga* shakes while being worshipped, then with thirteen thousand [pitchers]...
Then one shall attain purification. If [the deity] is to be worshipped on a Śivala [day], the Liṅga shall become pure by means of one hundred thousand water-pots.
If a Liṅga made of stone (śivātmake) is joined with a pedestal (vedīyukte) and has split into half-halves (ardhārdhasphuṭite),
it becomes pure by bathing the Liṅga after performing one hundred thousand ritual applications (lakṣaprayoga).
If the Liṅga were made of clay (kṛte)...
But for one who is afflicted by wind (vāta), no fault exists at the beginning.
If the Śivaliṅga should be seized or destroyed by Bhīma or other such defects,
then one should perform the appropriate expiation when it has been properly restored.
One should recite twenty thousand times, joined with a jarful of water.
Having performed [this], one shall attain purification.
If the linga, submerged in water, clearly becomes invisible,
then one who observes it with effort should perform an expiation.
Having offered five *apūpa* cakes to the jar of the *liṅga*,
and again offering five *yuta* [cakes], the breakage shall quickly be purified.
Now, O Lord, if the linga should be burnt and the fire itself be extinguished,
then this twice the penance must be performed by wise ascetics.
One should offer a blow to the neck of the sacrificial altar, a hundred jars to Śiva,
and the joining of the jar to the Liṅga;
this triad [should be performed] when a confluence of all sins has arisen.
Having awakened, one should practice renunciation and retain only what remains after giving;
for among all living beings, the yoga-machine is preeminent.
Therefore, a mendicant, regardless of his circumstances, should always practice that yoga.

"Having committed thousands of sins and having passed through various wombs, when Rudra has been released by one's devotion and is eternally united [with him], one does not perish. Thus ends the third chapter on the rules for expiation as taught by Gārgya-pāda.
If one stands in contact with a person who has eaten [impure food], bathing is prescribed by that rule; likewise, if one is touched by someone who is impure from eating,
one should perform the expiation after bowing with devotion to Śiva, the seer of the fivefold reality.
The supreme rite will be explained, which has been shown by the Gurus;
those [actions] which are to be extinguished first, as well as those which are to be avoided,
wherein all holy places, ablutions, and so forth entirely cease.
Anger, sorrow, delusion, and [the rest] are purified in that stainless state.
He ate alms-food.
In this manner, O seeker, when the direction has been determined and thoroughly examined,
and when it is seen again to be free from breath (nirucchvāsa), then one should commence the ritual action.
In every respect, I shall declare what must not be done by whom;
likewise, I shall state clearly, as it is prescribed in the scriptures, that which ought to be done, such as the ritual of bathing and so forth.
Having reached the further shore of the entire scripture in all its manifold details,
he was consecrated by the true teachers as one who embodies the form of the Teacher himself.
Then, one who has seen or heard the meaning, who serves many teachers,
who abides by the ritual rules, and who is skillful— such a person should perform his rite.

One should perform the ritual service for that patron who, according to his ability, has diligently applied himself to this path and by whom the state of the sun (the stage of Arhatship) has been attained.
They do not proceed toward other purposes or for the sake of crossing over;
nor should the rule regarding the flow [of the ritual] be performed by one who is ignorant of the scriptures.
Likewise, this sequence does not apply to all householders from the outset.
For those who have been initiated for the great sacrifices, it is appropriate for them in every respect.
The worship of one who is dead must be performed using vessels and so forth, as these are available;
if it were performed otherwise, it would be contradictory, being censured by both reasoning and scripture.
Just as the initiation and consecration must certainly be performed with diligence,
so too should one perform the meritorious *iṣṭi* rite according to the procedure— the supreme meaning of the scriptures— three times.
When the twice-born slay a deceased Brahmin who is without a protector,
the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice is ordained for those performers of meritorious deeds.
Just as it was there, so too here great merit is proclaimed;
having performed the rite according to the injunctions, one attains the yoga of Śiva.
Upon seeing a deceased person— whether it be one's guru, a disciple, or a Dharma brother—
one should not shed tears, for this is the path of all.
However, I shall explain in its entirety the ritual procedure that remains to be performed:
"Place white flowers, sandalwood paste, and thread;
likewise, [place] the vessel for the ashes and the water-pots."
Having gathered all of that together once more in a secluded, solitary place,
the wise preceptor should prepare three pedestals, smeared with cow dung, and provide a canopy for them.
One rite is for Śiva, and a second for the practitioner;
having performed the third, one should then ask forgiveness for whatever [faults] may have occurred.
The deceased should first be placed in water and smeared with perfumes and other substances;
one must not cause any defilement here, and one should also shave off the matted locks.
Afterwards, one should bathe [the deity] with ashes and then install it upon the bed once more.
One should construct a very extensive heap of ashes that is easy to approach;
this is prescribed as the ritual for both the Śiva-adept and the candidate at the time of initiation.
However, in the case of Rudra, one should perform it again, whereas for the candidate, the procedure is reversed.
One should strive to perform the ritual actions of both Śiva and the practitioner.
Having placed the second [element] there, one must necessarily apply the state of being (*bhāva*).
One [should perform the rite] with devotion to Śiva, while the second [should do so] for the sake of the practitioner;
having performed the ritual and drawn forth Śiva, he should then ask for forgiveness.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the practitioner according to the rule:
having placed Śivā to the north with her head toward the east,
and having meditated again upon Lakulīśa, one should thereafter perform the ritual action.
Having taken all the ritual substances and having placed the *pavitraka* in both hands, [one should proceed].
One should know the tips of the feet, the feet themselves, half of those [measures], and the knees; likewise the thighs, the penis, the hips, the abdomen,
the belly, the flanks, the armpits, the chest, and the back.

One should assign the shoulders, the neck, the mouth, the nose, the cheeks, and likewise the chin; the two eyes, the eyebrows, and the forehead; the two arms, the joints, the hands, the fingertips, and indeed everything else.
First the darbha grass, then ashes, sandalwood paste, and likewise the thread;
then flowers, and again incense—this is remembered as the sequence of the mantra. Furthermore, the practitioner performing the rite should indeed contemplate the mantras.

Standing before the form of Śiva, one should recite the mantra and, having produced a flash of light (*sphoṭa*), point it out. When the seventh or fifth flash occurs, whatever kind of transformation there may be for the practitioner, that supreme attainment has been proclaimed by Śiva himself.
Having thoroughly consecrated the *darbha* grass, sandalwood, flowers, and other items with mantras,

one should indeed cause them to circle the feet seven times; then, having offered fragrances, flowers, and unhusked rice (*akṣata*), one should place [the image] in each world-protector's station, and again on the second bed.
Having established it according to the rules and placed it auspiciously upon the head,
that object made of ash should be adorned with perfumes and flowers; however,
it must by no means be weighed in the presence of the practitioner.
Having thus performed the ritual for Kṛṣṇa, the preceptor, placing five or seven [offerings] before the practitioner, should with devotion ask Śiva for forgiveness.
Whatever has been done incorrectly, whether through ignorance or even through knowledge, may the Lord,
who is the cause of forgiveness for all those in the form of sacrificial animals, forgive all of that.
The practitioner shall describe [the procedure] in three ways: in water, in fire, and likewise on the ground.
Regarding water, it is prescribed in a great river; if that is not available, [it may be done] in any way whatsoever.
In the case of fire, [the body] must be cremated with many pieces of wood; there is no doubt in this matter.
O best of Brahmins, let the Śūdras purify even the six classes in any way possible; furthermore, someone who gives alms, or one who, by family tradition, bears the banner and garlands,
should perform the consecration according to the prescribed number and so forth with devotion, as it has been ordained.
On the ground, one should dig a pit for the practitioner according to his own measurement;
its width is said to be half of that, because otherwise faults are observed.
Indeed, illness may arise as a hardship, and there is a longing for what is excessive.
Therefore, one should never do more than this;
having worshipped with flowers in a beautiful pit, the practitioner should then cast [the offering] back in.
Or else, the filling-in (pūraṇa) should be performed for Lakulīśa as well, according to the rule.
The purifying thread, the book, the disciple, and some staff or similar object, in due order.
That which was prepared should then be given to the preceptor;
furthermore, one should not, out of greed, give anything to a relative.
This is the essential wealth of those who perform penance, without a doubt.
In this world, whatever is known everywhere as being without self, one should not commit evil; for life is indeed impermanent. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the individual.
